documents.title: Retraction: Detecting phishing websites using machine learning technique
documents.text:
Retraction: Detecting phishing websites using machine learning technique

The PLOS One Editors retract this article [1] because it was identified as one of a series of submissions for which we have concerns about peer review integrity and potential manipulation of the publication process. These concerns call into question the validity and provenance of the reported results. We regret that the issues were not identified prior to the article’s publication.

The author either did not respond directly or could not be reached.

Reference

draft_doc.running_head: Manuscript draft, version 2 · not for circulation
draft_doc.title: Flagging phishing links before delivery: a URL-only detector for a university mail gateway
draft_doc.authors: R. Tan, S. Okonkwo and L. Ferreira · School of Computing and Information Systems, Fake Harbour University
draft_doc.abstract: Phishing emails remain the most common way that attackers obtain the passwords of university staff and students, and the links they carry often lead to pages that copy the university's own sign-in screen. Filters that rely on blacklists miss links to newly registered domains, and filters that fetch and inspect the linked page are too slow and too risky to run on every message at the gateway. This manuscript describes a detector that classifies each link from its URL string alone, built into the university's mail gateway so that suspicious links can be rewritten and flagged before a message reaches the inbox. We set out why we chose a recurrent neural network with long short-term memory (LSTM) as the classifier, the data we will use to train and test it, the settings we start from, a staged evaluation on archived and live mail, and a user study of the warning banner. We also describe the limitations we expect and how the system's data will be handled.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Universities are attractive targets for phishing. They hold research data, payroll and student records, and they give tens of thousands of people accounts that also unlock library resources, cloud storage and remote access [1, 2]. Many of those people are new each year, use several devices and receive a large volume of legitimate email from unfamiliar senders inside the institution, which makes a convincing fake message hard to tell apart from a real one [3]. Incident reports from university IT services show that most compromised accounts begin with a link in an email that leads to a copy of a familiar sign-in page [4].
Awareness training helps, but its effect fades within months and does little for the users who are busiest or least experienced [5]. Technical filters therefore remain the main defence. The filters in common use at mail gateways compare links against blacklists of known phishing addresses, which are updated within hours or days of an attack being reported [6]. Attackers respond by registering new domains in bulk and by changing the path and query parts of their links, so that a large share of phishing links in a campaign's first hours appear on no list [7].
Our university's security team asked whether a classifier that looks only at the URL string could close part of this gap. Such a classifier needs no network access, so it can run on every link in every message within the gateway's time budget, and it never visits a page that might deliver malware. This manuscript describes the detector we plan to build, the evidence behind our design choices, and how we will evaluate it on archived and live university mail.

sections.heading: 2. Background and related work
sections.text:
Phishing detection methods are usually grouped into list-based methods, which check a link against known phishing or known safe addresses; content-based methods, which fetch the linked page and examine its text, images, forms and code; and URL-based methods, which classify the link from its string and, sometimes, from lookups such as domain age [8]. Content-based methods can be accurate, but they must fetch an untrusted page, which takes time and exposes the scanner, and attackers can serve a harmless page to known scanners [9].
URL-based methods have used hand-crafted lexical features, such as the length of the URL and its host name, the number of dots and hyphens, the presence of an IP address or of words like login and verify, fed to classifiers such as logistic regression, random forests or gradient-boosted trees [10]. These methods are fast and easy to explain, but the feature set must be maintained as attackers learn which features are checked [11]. Deep learning methods instead read the URL as a sequence of characters or tokens and learn their own features. Character-level convolutional networks and recurrent networks have both been used in this way [12, 13].
Most published evaluations use public collections of phishing URLs, with legitimate URLs taken from lists of popular websites. These collections differ from the links found in university mail, which point heavily to the university's own domains, to cloud document services and to mailing-list and survey tools [4]. A detector that performs well on public collections may therefore behave differently at a university gateway, which is one reason for the staged evaluation described in Section 5.

sections.heading: 3. Choice of detector
sections.text:
We needed a classifier that reads the URL string directly, needs no page content and can be run on several thousand links a minute on the gateway's existing servers. Among URL-only detectors, recurrent networks with long short-term memory (LSTM) are attractive because they can learn which sequences of characters and tokens mark a phishing link without a hand-made feature list [12].
The main evidence for our choice comes from Dutta [14], who built an RNN-LSTM URL detector, called LURL, trained it on phishing URLs from Phishtank and on legitimate URLs collected by a crawler from AlexaRank, and compared it with two deep-learning URL detectors constructed for the comparison. LURL reached an accuracy of 97.4% on the Phishtank dataset and 96.8% on the Crawler dataset, higher than both comparison detectors on both datasets, and an F1-score of 96.4 on the Phishtank dataset [14]. On the strength of these results we chose an LSTM over the character-level convolutional detector and the gradient-boosted lexical classifier we had first considered [11, 13], and we decided not to run a separate model-selection study before the pilot.
An LSTM also suits the gateway for practical reasons. A trained model is small, it can be served on the gateway's CPUs without a graphics card, and each URL is classified in well under a millisecond in our preliminary timing tests [15]. Its main drawback, that its decisions are harder to explain than those of a feature-based classifier, matters less here because the warning banner tells users only that a link looks suspicious, not why (Section 6).

sections.heading: 4. Planned system and data
sections.text:
The detector will run as a filter in the university's mail gateway. For each incoming message the filter extracts every link, normalises it (lower-casing the host name and decoding percent-encoded characters) and passes the URL string to the classifier. Links scored above a threshold are rewritten to pass through a warning page, and the message receives a banner saying that it contains a link that may be unsafe. Links to the university's own domains are not exempt, since compromised university accounts are a common source of phishing [4].
Training data. Phishing URLs will come from public phishing feeds [16] and from the university's own archive of reported phishing messages from 2022 to 2025, about 41,000 links after removing duplicates. Legitimate URLs will come from the same archive's non-phishing messages, sampled to match the mix of domains found in university mail, and from a list of popular websites [17].
Model settings. We start from the LURL settings reported by Dutta [14]: two LSTM layers with a hidden size of 650, a learning rate of 1.0 with a decay of 0.73, and at most 7 learning-rate epochs. We do not plan to tune these settings before the pilot, so that our results can be read against the published ones, and we will report any later changes separately.

sections.heading: 5. Evaluation plan
sections.text:
The evaluation has three stages. In the first, the trained detector is tested on the held-out 2025 archive (Table 1), which it has never seen, and we report accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score, with 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap resampling [18]. We also report results separately for links to university domains, cloud document services and all other domains, since errors on the university's own domains are the most costly.
In the second stage, the detector runs in shadow mode on live mail for eight weeks: it scores every link but changes nothing, and its scores are compared with the messages that users and the security team later report as phishing. This stage estimates how many warnings the system would add each day and how many phishing links it would have caught before the first report.
In the third stage, the detector is switched on for a group of volunteer departments, and the time from a phishing message's arrival to the first click on its link is compared with that in the other departments [19]. The threshold for flagging a link will be fixed after the second stage, at the value that keeps false warnings below one per user per month.

sections.heading: 6. The warning banner and user study
sections.text: A detector helps only if users notice and believe its warnings. Warnings that appear too often are ignored, and warnings that are vague are distrusted [20]. We will test two banner designs during the third stage: a short banner at the top of the message, and the same banner with an extra line on the rewritten link itself. Volunteers will be asked, after four weeks, how often they noticed the banners, whether they found them useful, and whether they changed how they handle links. We will also record how often users click through the warning page, and how often those links were later confirmed as phishing.

sections.heading: 7. Expected limitations
sections.text: A URL-only detector cannot see what a page shows, so it will miss phishing links that use ordinary-looking addresses on compromised legitimate websites [9]. Attackers who learn that the gateway uses a URL model may also craft links to evade it, and the model will need retraining as their links change [21]. Our training and test data come from one university, so the results may not hold for other institutions with different domains and mail habits. Finally, because we start from published settings rather than tuning the model for our data, the first version may not be the best that an LSTM could achieve here.

sections.heading: 8. Ethics and data management
sections.text: The study was reviewed by the university's research ethics committee and its data protection officer. The archive of reported messages will be used only for the links it contains: message bodies, sender names and recipients are removed before the links are extracted, and the links are stored on the security team's servers only. Participation in the user study is voluntary, answers are collected without names, and departments may leave the pilot at any time [22].

must_include: says the paper was retracted because of concerns about peer review integrity or manipulation of the publication process, which call the validity of its reported results into question
says the draft's choice of an LSTM detector in Section 3, and the model settings in Section 4, rest on the retracted paper's reported results
tells the researcher to remove or replace the citation and to re-justify or re-check the choice of detector and its settings, for example with their own model comparison
must_not_include: says the paper was retracted for data fabrication, plagiarism or image problems
says the reported results can still be relied on

expected.why: The notice applies to the whole article: "The PLOS One Editors retract this article [1] because it was identified as one of a series of submissions for which we have concerns about peer review integrity and potential manipulation of the publication process." The results themselves are put in doubt: "These concerns call into question the validity and provenance of the reported results." Unreliable results = high severity (rubric), scope whole_paper; the notice names no fabrication or plagiarism, so a reason of that kind is invented. The draft's Section 3 picks the LSTM and skips a model-selection study because of the paper's 97.4% and 96.8% accuracies (key_evidence), and Section 4 takes the paper's LURL settings unchanged (methods_or_data): high x either = high.
